s: Repose is a perfect, unchanging level of the universe and the Sage’s mental equilibrium, not ordinary inactivity. Established inwardly, it produces movement, attainment, inaction, potential action, happiness, long life, wisdom, and knowledge. With passivity it excludes sorrow, anxiety, foul influences, plans, and worldly disturbance; through it, ancients cultivated TAO, developing harmony and order.

TAO of inaction is happiness, true pleasure, and the path to perfect happiness and preservation of life. Through non-doing and inner repose, it spontaneously produces action, changes things through Heaven and Earth, accomplishes all things, leaves nothing undone, and preserves the ruler’s energy.

Happiness is found in contentment and is complete when desire is attained, with nothing further to add. Yet it is not exempt from sorrow: office and its absence cause unhappiness. In the human world it is uncertain whether common happiness, following the majority, is real; wealth and reputation bring attachment, anxiety, and fear.

visits Lao Tzŭ [to ask about personal cultivation] Shih Ch'êng Ch'i first accuses Lao Tzŭ of lacking charity and being stingy, then apologizes when Lao Tzŭ remains silent. Lao Tzŭ criticizes his self-satisfied, hasty, and overconfident manner, saying such men are not trusted.

follow TAO [in the sequence of apprehension] Forms and names arise after earlier stages in the understanding of TAO. To rise directly to them is to ignore their source, and using them without understanding the great principle gives only the instrumental part of government.

follow forms and names [in the sequence of government] Rewards and punishments are the lowest form of education. They should be considered only after the earlier phases of TAO, forms, names, capabilities, and distinctions have been understood.

makes wheels [by coordinating mind and hand through mysterious art] The wheelwright interrupts Duke Huan’s reading and argues that the words of dead Sages are only their dregs. He explains through wheel-making that a mysterious coordination of mind and hand cannot be taught through words, even to his son.

Wên Wang, called a sage, seeks to employ the old man of Tsang in government and invokes a supposed dream to satisfy ministers and the vulgar. After the administration succeeds, he appoints the old man Grand Tutor and asks about extending government over the empire.

l: Confucius's attainment of TAO, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Confucius's attainment of TAO follows three months at home after speaking with Lao Tzŭ, ending in recognition that natural developments follow fixed laws and enlightenment cannot be given by the unenlightened.
Self-conceit is personal over-estimation, expressed through social withdrawal, distinction, tall talk, and abuse of others.
Spirituality is a pure, simple state extending everywhere. Preserved without loss, it unites a person with itself, operates freely, and brings that person into relationship with God.
Passivity places the Sage in repose, preventing sorrow and anxiety while allowing virtue and spirituality to remain complete and unimpaired.

wear scholars' robes [not necessarily those with TAO] Scholars who wear round hats are said to know the seasons of Heaven, those with square shoes know the shape of Earth, and those with loose girdles are ready to decide questions. The text distinguishes genuine scholars who have TAO from people who merely wear scholars' robes.
Primeval man lives in perfect tranquillity and unity, with ordered seasons and united principles, possessing knowledge yet never needing to use it.
Retired scholars preserve themselves when their age makes their mission unsuitable; after success they efface themselves in unity, but after failure rely on themselves and wait.
Office, once seen as external and not desire’s attainment, later became identified with it despite causing unhappiness.

l: Spirit of the River, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Spirit of the River rejoices in autumn floods and thinks earth’s beauty is his; traveling eastward downstream to the ocean, he recognizes the Spirit of the Ocean as superior and learns his insignificance and the relativity of distinctions.

l: Spirit of the Ocean, Chuang Tzŭ
s: receives river [as a speaker seeking instruction] The Spirit of the Ocean teaches the Spirit of the River about the limits of individual knowledge, the endlessness of time and space, and the relativity of dimensions and values. He explains TAO, the natural and artificial, and the need to let all things take their course.

is_a seasonal flooding The autumn floods cause every stream to pour into the river and make the river swell greatly. They begin the Spirit of the River's journey toward recognition of his own limitations.
has no reputation The man of TAO has no reputation, and perfect virtue acquires nothing. Those who understand TAO do not suffer injury from without because they let all things take their course.
The truly great man practices self-discipline, avoids injuring others and seeking gain, asks no help or credit, and remains unmoved by worldly rank, punishment, or shame.

Greatness and smallness are relative, without fixed extremes or limits. The wise person avoids treating either as excessive or deficient. Greatness is not secured by talk or great deeds, but by seeking and rejecting nothing, avoiding injury, and finding safety according to nature.
are limitless Dimensions are limitless, and terms describing them are not final. Both small and great things possess form, but no thing can be called absolutely the greatest or smallest.

are relative [from the point of view of TAO] Value and worthlessness have no absolute extremes from the point of view of TAO. Their determination depends on perspective, conditions, opportunity, and the impartial embrace of all creation.
The frog lives happily in an old well, believing its limited surroundings unsurpassed, until a turtle describes the vast eastern sea, leaving it astonished and unable to answer.
Walrus envies centipede’s many legs and nimble gait, unsuccessfully hops on one leg, and asks how it manages them.
Centipede has many legs, moves naturally without conscious management, explains this to snake, and admits it cannot match snake’s legless speed.
Snake moves quickly without legs, has form and wriggles; the centipede envies it, while it contrasts itself with formless wind.
is_caused_by fate Failure is described by Confucius as something determined by fate. In the days of Yao and Shun, no one throughout the empire was a failure, though no one recognized the gain.
is opportunity Success is described by Confucius as depending on opportunity. In the days of Chieh and Chou, no one throughout the empire was a success, though no one recognized the loss.

Kung Sun Lung, a Chao State philosopher and sophist dialectician, writes on the “hard and white.” Though he claims mastery of many doctrines and arguments, hearing Chuang Tzŭ leaves him astonished, speechless, and humbled.
State of Chao goes to rack and ruin within three years as other princes form designs upon it.

is_a person [of Wei] Mou of Wei listens to Kung Sun Lung’s request to explain the secret of Chuang Tzŭ’s grandeur. He responds by describing the frog in the old well, the turtle of the eastern sea, and the limits of narrow knowledge.

l: turtle of the eastern sea, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Turtle of the eastern sea has great happiness, cannot enter a well when its legs become stuck, retreats, and describes the eastern sea’s vastness and constancy through flood and drought.
The eastern sea is immeasurably broad and deep, its volume unchanged by years of flood or drought.

The sacred tortoise of Ch’u has been dead about three thousand years; its remains are kept in a chest on an ancestral altar, illustrating that living and wagging its tail in mud surpasses posthumous veneration.
A bird of the south flies from the southern sea to the northern sea, stopping only on wu-t’ung trees to eat bamboo fruit and drink pure spring water; an owl screeches as it passes.

l: bridge over the Hao, Chuang Tzŭ
s: is_over Hao The bridge over the Hao is where Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ stroll when Chuang Tzŭ remarks on the pleasure of the minnows. Chuang Tzŭ says that he knows this pleasure from his own feelings on the bridge.

are darting about [in the Hao] The minnows are seen darting about beneath the bridge over the Hao. Chuang Tzŭ calls their movement pleasurable, while Hui Tzŭ questions how he can know their pleasure without being a fish.

have pleasure [as inferred from the minnows darting about] The fishes become the subject of the debate between Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ. Hui Tzŭ argues that Chuang Tzŭ cannot know their pleasure because he is not a fish, while Chuang Tzŭ says he infers it from his own feelings on the bridge.
Perfect happiness is a state of inaction, sought with preservation of life, yet described as absent happiness; death is claimed happier than kingship.

is_a worldly aim [what the world aims at] Physical well-being is used to judge the world’s pursuits of wealth, rank, old age, goodness, comfort, rich food, fine clothes, beauty, and music. The text says people can generally live well without these extras.
Kuan Chung, Duke Huan’s charioteer and minister, dies after advising the visiting duke not to appoint Pao Yü, recommending Hsi P'êng to administer the State.
A bleached, shape-preserving empty skull represents death; in Chuang Tzŭ’s dream it praises freedom from mortal troubles and rejects restoration to mortal relationships.

l: The Secret of Life, Chuang Tzŭ
s: A chapter supplement teaches that true fitness unfolds through simultaneous care of the internal self, vitality, and physical body.
Vitality is an immaterial essence uniting with matter to produce life, dissipated by anger, preserved by inner care, and restored through concentration and harmony.

The internal self requires constant care alongside the physical body. Shan Pao cared for his inner self but neglected his external man, while Chang I cared externally but neglected the internal self; both failed to care for the lagging part.

Kuan Yin is presented as a sage and, in some accounts, Lao Tzŭ’s disciple entrusted with publishing the Tao-Tê-Ching. He teaches that perfection comes from absolute purity rather than cunning, and that the perfect man gains security through unity, inner strength, harmonized virtue, and partnership with God. An enthusiastic follower of TAO, he builds a system on nothingness and ONE, advocating gentleness, humility, receptivity, non-aggression, and situational response. The text calls him a true Sage.

The perfect man is a person of absolute purity who unites physical frame, vitality, nature, and virtue with God. Formless and beyond objective existences, he vanquishes death, passes unharmed through solid bodies and fire, scales heights without fear, and acts without reliance on self-confidence or authority. He shares earthly food while sharing God’s happiness, remains free from care, and avoids trouble, censure, plotting, and toadying. Though he may be hidden, he benefits both natural and artificial things and enters God’s eternal harmony. In the end, he leaves no trace, transcends human limits without leaving the world, and lives with mankind unharmed and inwardly independent.
A huge, foliage-covered tree is deemed useless to woodsmen and therefore remains standing to complete its allotted span.
The goose is distinguished by cackling; if it does not cackle, it is deemed useless, selected for slaughter, and killed.

is_a hindrance [in oneself] The human element is described as a hindrance within oneself and a source of sorrow in others. I Liao says that the great Yao lacked this element and advises the prince of Lu to put off the hindrance and roam with TAO.

advises prince of Lu [to put away body and skin and purge passion] I Liao, identified as a sage of the Ch'u State, advises the prince of Lu that worldly efforts cannot secure freedom from misfortune. He urges the prince to discard power, lessen desires, and trust in TAO.
An unoccupied boat crossing a river causes no anger when it collides, illustrating that roaming empty through life makes injury difficult.
A minister to Duke Ling of Wei, Pei Kung Shê raises voluntary contributions for bells and completes them in three months without resentment, gratitude, or injury.

are_hung altar [upper and lower bells after three months] The bells, upper and lower, are all hung after three months of contributions. Their completion is attributed to Pei Kung Shê's non-interference and lack of resentment or gratitude.
is_a park [where Chuang Tzŭ wandered] Tiao-ling is the park where Chuang Tzŭ sees a strange bird in a chestnut grove. After the encounter, Chuang Tzŭ avoids leaving his house for three months.
The strange bird, with a seven-foot wingspan and inch-wide eyes, pursues prey near Chuang Tzŭ, forgets its nature, and becomes prey itself.

leads_to rank and power [when adapting to surroundings] Adaptation to surroundings is described as bringing rank and power, though such advantages are external and not derived from oneself. The swallow illustrates adaptation by avoiding unsuitable places and dwelling among men where it finds its natural abode.

l: the dilemma of usefulness, Chuang Tzŭ
s: is_resolved_by TAO [halfway between usefulness and uselessness] The dilemma contrasts the huge tree, which survives because it is useless, with the goose, which dies because it is useless. Chuang Tzŭ rests halfway between usefulness and uselessness, but says that only TAO provides a fixed point beyond the dilemma.

is_a burial [in the natural order of Established-Virtue] Death is described as the end that the Sage quietly awaits and as the point at which man is reunited with God. In the district called Established-Virtue, life is for enjoyment and death is for burial.

l: siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, Chuang Tzŭ
s: During the siege between Ch'ên and Ts'ai, Confucius goes seven days without food. The experience leads to discussions of fear of death, adaptation, God, and the dangers of displaying knowledge and seeking fame.

T'ien Tzŭ Fang attends Prince Wên of Wei, repeatedly praises Ch'i Kung’s discourse on TAO, and identifies his tutor Tung Kuo Shun Tzŭ as perfect, pure, unconditioned, and able to awaken people to error.

l: Prince Wên of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Prince Wên of Wei, tutored by T'ien Tzŭ Fang, shifts from valuing formal morality to seeing prior learning and ruling Wei as limiting and harmful.

l: Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ
s: A sage from the south, Wên Po Hsüeh Tzŭ visits Lu on journeys to and from Ch'i, initially refusing a Lu man for lacking human-heart knowledge, then twice meeting him and lamenting his rigid, admonishing conduct.
An unseen, unwitnessed source whose report fills space, possibly produces creation, and may explain darkness, light, recurring time, life, death, and continual production.

l: Duke Ai of Lu, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Duke Ai of Lu, ruler of Lu, claims many scholars based on robes; challenged by Chuang Tzŭ, he threatens false wearers, leaving one old man.

l: Prince Yüan of Sung, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Prince Yüan of Sung dreams of a marine messenger, consults soothsayers, summons Yü Ch'ieh, and kills a captured white tortoise for divination after an auspicious response.

l: old man of Tsang, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The old man of Tsang, appointed Grand Tutor by Wên Wang, governs without changing statutes or unjust rules; after three years order and unified interests emerge, then he refuses Wên Wang and disappears.

is_unfit_for Tzŭ Chou Chih Fu [because he would do nothing in the way of government] Government is described as less important than self-culture and as merely the surplus or dregs of TAO. The unit suggests that only one who would do nothing in the way of government is fit to be trusted with the empire.

l: Po Hun Wu Jên, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Po Hun Wu Jên, a perfect man in archery and composure, judges Lieh Yü K'ou, tests him under danger, and demonstrates fearless unchanged composure at a precipice.

Sun Shu Ao stays emotionally steady through three appointments and dismissals, treating rank and power as outside himself. At a banquet he stands quietly in repose; the men of Ying throw down their arms. His inaction, rather than speech, is presented as effective from office to banquet.

does_not_disturb Sun Shu Ao [because it is outside his own self] Rank and power are treated as worldly conditions that do not affect a person who has TAO. The perfect sages and Sun Shu Ao remain unmoved by obtaining or losing office, and honour is said to reside in the person rather than in a changing condition.
Prince of Fan, protected by TAO beyond mundane influences, says Fan State’s destruction did not injure his existence, unlike the Prince of Ch'u’s dependence on his state.

is_destroyed Prince of Fan [without injuring his existence] The destruction of the Fan State is presented as insufficient to injure the existence of the Prince of Fan. The state is contrasted with the individual existence that TAO places beyond mundane influences.
Knowledge, a being, asks how TAO may be known, approached, and attained; unanswered and told an answer is forgotten, it is judged wholly wrong by the Yellow Emperor.
A being who cannot answer Knowledge’s questions about TAO is later called genuinely right by the Yellow Emperor for not knowing.
A being who, while answering Knowledge, forgets his words; this forgetting places him near TAO, and he later approves the Yellow Emperor’s words.

The universe is beautiful and silent, with four seasons abiding by fixed law and grounded in absolute principles. It is immeasurably great, rejects nothing, and its evolutions, deaths, births, forms, and transformations exceed human intellect. It serves as a standard of greatness, while TAO purifies, nourishes, and encompasses it and all creation. Specialists wrongly claim exclusive definition of its beauty and principles. Hui Tzŭ loves and investigates all creation endlessly, yet does not reach a conclusion in TAO.
Vital fluid produces life through convergence and death through dispersion, with life described as its concentration of barely varying duration.

Nan Yung Ch'u, a disciple troubled by moral dilemmas, seeks TAO and the art of preserving life. He first hears TAO only with his ears, cultivates good and eliminates evil within himself, then seeks further instruction from Kêng Sang Ch'u and Lao Tzŭ after self-cultivation leaves him confused.
Portal of God is Non-Existence, a formless passage through which one enters and leaves, from which all things arise.

is_a virtue [the basis of virtue passive and virtue active] Spontaneity is essential to TAO and is expressed through natural, unforced emotion and action. Perfect politeness, duty, wisdom, charity, and trust are described as spontaneous rather than artificial or calculated. The Sage follows necessity, which is the TAO of the Sage.

l: art of preserving life, Chuang Tzŭ
s: consists_in inaction [by which there is nothing that cannot be accomplished] The art of preserving life consists in keeping all in ONE, losing nothing, knowing when to stop and how much is enough, leaving others alone, attending to oneself, and remaining without cares and excessive knowledge. It is illustrated by the child, whose constitutional harmony allows it to act, move, and adapt without conscious calculation. Lao Tzŭ later connects it with freedom from trouble, repose, and unconscious adaptation to circumstances.

l: subjective point of view, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The subjective point of view originates in life, with knowledge as tutor, and develops into personal judgments of right and wrong. It mistakes individual standards for universal ones, values usefulness and success narrowly, and remains fallible.
Existence proceeds from Non-Existence, has unlimited Space and beginningless Time, and unfolds through birth and death as stages in the ultimate unity of existence and Non-Existence.

A hermit introduced by Nü Shang visits Wu Hou of Wei, condemns passions and artificial love and duty as harmful sources of disorder, advocates inward sincerity and non-aggression, and teaches the Prince that nourishment and spiritual health matter to rulers and common people alike.

l: Wu Hou of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Wu Hou of Wei, a prince whose sensual rule oppresses people, seeks to love them and end war but is warned his duty-based approach will be disastrous.

introduces Hsü Wu Kuei Nü Shang introduces Hsü Wu Kuei to Wu Hou of Wei and later questions him about the words that pleased the Prince. Hsü Wu Kuei explains that the Prince was moved by hearing about dogs and horses and by encountering the voice of a pure man.

Horses of the State have straightness, curve, squareness, and roundness, but horses of the Empire outstrip them, moving as though parted with individuality. Hsü Wu Kuei presents them as levels of natural excellence, whose care requires preventing harm.

l: love for the people, Chuang Tzŭ
s: is the root of all evil to the people Hsü Wu Kuei calls love for the people the root of all evil to the people when adopted as a deliberate governing project. He says that such an intention produces artificial and potentially harmful outward conduct.

originates_in duty towards one's neighbour [when cultivated to put an end to war] War is said to arise from attempts to cultivate duty towards one's neighbour as a means of ending conflict. Hsü Wu Kuei argues that sincere abstention and non-aggression can spare the people death without requiring a separate effort to end war.

Hsi P'êng is recommended as administrator of the State, yet forgets superiors’ authority, causes inferiors to forget his, grieves over those below him, and ignores some minor State and family matters.
is_located_at Hsiang-ch'êng [beyond the wilds] Chü-tz'ŭ Mountain is the place where the Yellow Emperor goes to see TAO. The Yellow Emperor's party loses its way while travelling there.
A horse herder guides the Yellow Emperor, knows where TAO abides, and teaches that governing an empire means preventing harm, like caring for horses.
requires no harm comes to the horses Horses' natural care consists in ensuring that no harm comes to the horses. The boy presents this simple protection as the model for governing the empire.

Dialecticians regarded Hui Tzŭ as a great philosopher and subtle dialectician, then argued endlessly over his paradoxes. Including Huan T'uan and Kung Sun Lung, they used specious premises to impose false conclusions, winning verbal battles without convincing adversaries.

are not general [when each man has his own] Moral standards are questioned through the debate between Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ. Chuang Tzŭ suggests that if every person had an individual standard of right, everyone could be called Yao, exposing the difficulty of competing standards.
The people, a social class symbolized by a sword, suffer rulers’ oppression but can escape death when a ruler rejects aggression and cultivates inward sincerity.

Pao Yü is a pure, incorruptible, good man who avoids unlike people and remembers wrongdoing; Kuan Chung says that, if employed in governing the empire, these traits would make him quarrel with Duke Huan and the people.
contains monkeys [in its thicket] Monkey Mountain is visited and ascended by the prince of Wu. Its monkeys flee when they see him.
Yen Pu I studies under Tung Wu to remove superiority, abandons pleasures and reputation, receives warnings against flaunting superiority, and becomes widely praised after three years.
is_a professor of TAO Tung Wu is a professor of TAO who teaches Yen Pu I to overcome his displayed superiority.

l: I Liao of Shih-nan, Chuang Tzŭ
s: I Liao of Shih-nan, a Sage under menial garb, pours a banquet libation and plays with his ball while two houses’ trouble is arranged.
Confucius presents wordless utterances as a doctrine that, through silence, achieves greater results than speech.
is_a physiognomist Chiu Fang Yin examines Tzŭ Chi's sons physiognomically and predicts that K'un will be fortunate because he will eat at a prince's table.
K'un is judged fortunate as a son who will eat at a prince's table, but is captured by brigands, loses his feet, and ends as door-keeper to Duke Chü in Ch'i State.

l: K'un's capture by brigands, Chuang Tzŭ
s: results_in loss of feet [before sale into Ch'i State] K'un's capture by brigands results in his feet being cut off because he is difficult to sell otherwise. He is then sold into the Ch'i State and made a door-keeper to Duke Chü.
The divine man avoids both excessive intimacy and distance from crowds, dislikes diversity that hinders advantage, clings to virtue and harmony, and trusts natural events over artificial measures.
encamps_at Kuei-ch'i [with three thousand armed warriors] Kou Chien encamps with three thousand armed warriors at Kuei-ch'i while leading the men of Wu against the Yüeh State.
Chung Wên alone sees that defeat will be followed by a rally, but he cannot foresee the evil that will later come upon himself.
Tsê Yang visits Ch'u seeking the prince’s interview, is refused, asks Wang Kuo, and is directed instead to Kung Yüeh Hsiu.
Kung Yüeh Hsiu is a hermit who catches turtles in winter and rests in a mountain copse in summer; knowledgeable without virtue, arrogance prevents influencing the prince.

l: Prince Hui of Wei, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Prince Hui of Wei, ruler of Wei State, considers assassinating prince Wei of Ch'i after a broken treaty, then reconsiders through Tai Chin Jen's snail-horn kingdoms image.
Tai Chin Jen, a Sage of the Liang State, advises Prince Hui by comparing Wei and Liang to snail-horn kingdoms, diminishing petty rulers against boundless space.
Poh Chü studies under Lao Tzŭ, criticises contemporary rulers, and urges wandering while condemning burdens and punishments that foster crime.

asks_about society Shao Chih asks T'ai Kung Tiao about society, TAO, the vitality of things, and whether Chance or Predestination is correct. He receives explanations that distinguish conditioned material existence from the infinite nature of TAO.

defines society [as an agreement of families and individuals] T'ai Kung Tiao defines society as an agreement among families and individuals whose different elements form a whole. He explains that the Positive and Negative principles, the seasons, and opposing conditions generate change, while Chance and Predestination are both inadequate explanations.
Society is an agreement of families and individuals to follow customs, uniting distinct and discordant elements into a harmonious whole.
Chance is a prior explanation limited to conditioned material existences, rejected because it implies absolute absence of principle and cannot account for the infinite.
Predestination explains conditioned material existences and implies a real existence, but T'ai Kung Tiao rejects its beginning as unable to explain infinity or pre-matter.

are_uncertain uncertain Contingencies are uncertain, and external events such as life, death, loyalty, filial piety, success, and worldly reputation lie beyond reliable control. The unit contrasts these with the inner self, which alone can be controlled without harm.

Jên Kung Tzŭ, a young noble of the Jen State, fishes at Kuei-chi with a huge hook, big line, and fifty oxen as bait. After a year he catches and salts a great fish that feeds many; his example contrasts with minor ability seeking small positions.
Lao Lai Tzŭ, a sage of the Ch'u State, urges Confucius to abandon dogmatism, specious knowledge, and influence-seeking goodness, teaching selfless action without claiming success.
catches divine tortoise [in a net] Yü Ch'ieh is a fisherman who catches a white tortoise five feet in semi-circumference. His net captures the tortoise despite its divine status.

A white tortoise five feet in semi-circumference appears in Prince Yüan of Sung’s dream, is identified, trapped despite wisdom, killed and cut to pieces, then yields seventy-two faultless omens for divination.

l: Tung Kuo Tzŭ Chi, Chuang Tzŭ
s: instructs Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu Tung Kuo Tzŭ Chi received Yen Ch'êng Tzŭ Yu’s account of his gradual development and reflections on life, death, Heaven, Earth, and Destiny.

l: Tzŭ Chou Chih Fu, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Tzŭ Chou Chih Fu declines Yao’s offer of the empire, citing a troublesome disease and efforts to cure it, though he is considered fit to be trusted with it.
Shan Chüan declines Shun’s empire, prefers agricultural work, rest, and light-hearted contentment, wears seasonal simple clothes, and ultimately hides among the mountains.

l: T'ai Wang Shan Fu, Chuang Tzŭ
s: T'ai Wang Shan Fu occupies Pin and, when savages attack, offers valuables but abandons territory rather than risk lives. He leads his people to Mount Ch'i’s foot and founds a new State, showing respect for preservation of life.
Yüeh, Prince Chao’s butcher, follows him into exile, declines restored salary and further rewards after the kingdom returns, refuses office and audience, and goes back to butchery.

knows_difference_between gain [and what is important] Tzŭ Hua Tzŭ told prince Chao Hsi that the body was more important than the empire and that the disputed territory was of still less importance. He taught that the prince was exhausting himself over something comparatively insignificant.

l: Prince Chao of the Ch'u State, Chuang Tzŭ
s: loses_and_recovers the loss and restoration of the Ch'u kingdom [with Yüeh following him into exile] Prince Chao of the Ch'u State lost his kingdom and went into exile with Yüeh, then recovered it and distributed rewards to those who had remained faithful.

dwells_in the State of Lu [in a poor mud hut] Yüan Hsien lived in extreme poverty but maintained that he was merely poor, not defective. He rejected self-promotion, flattering friendships, learning for others, teaching for himself, and displaying horses and carriages.
Pien Sui refuses to advise T'ang on attacking Chieh, rejects the empire to avoid appearing covetous, and drowns himself in the river Chou.

rise_in the rise of the Chou dynasty The Chous were criticized for taking power after the iniquities of the Yins through intrigue, bribery, mobilized troops, treaty sacrifices, and fighting. Po I and Shu Ch'i judged the Chous' rule to be a disgrace and fled from it.

l: the loss and restoration of the Ch'u kingdom, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The loss and restoration of the Ch'u kingdom caused Prince Chao of the Ch'u State to go into exile and later recover his throne. Yüeh followed him but accepted no extra reward after regaining his own butchery.

l: the attack on Chieh, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The attack on Chieh was undertaken by T'ang after consultations with Pien Sui, Wu Kuang, and I Yin, and it ended in Chieh's defeat. Pien Sui and Wu Kuang condemned the political and moral implications of the attack and refused the empire afterward.

l: the rise of the Chou dynasty, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The rise of the Chou dynasty was judged by Po I and Shu Ch'i to involve intrigue, bribery, violence, and disorder rather than TAO. They rejected association with it and starved themselves at Mount Shou-yang.
Liu Hsia Chi, a virtuous Lu official and Robber Chê’s much older elder brother, warns Confucius against visiting Robber Chê and later confirms Confucius was rebuffed.
number nine thousand Robber Chê's followers number nine thousand and assist him as he ravages the empire and plunders nobles and households.

Original purity is God-given, unchangeable truth unalloyed; it necessarily grounds human emotions and responses, including grief, awe, friendship, filial service, and loyalty, and is esteemed by the true Sage.

l: Confucius's visit to Robber Chê, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Confucius’s visit sends respectful messages to Robber Chê, ends in verbal rebuff, and leaves Confucius distressed after nearly entering the tiger’s mouth.
Tzŭ Chang asks Man Kou Tê, seeking reputation through virtue, and argues that neighbourly duty brings confidence, wealth, social place, and moral distinction.
Man Kou Tê seeks wealth, dismisses shame, and values confidence for notice, arguing rulers and ministers prosper through immorality and virtue lacks scope without reputation and wealth.
Wu Yoh, an arbitrator, contrasts the mean man’s pursuit of wealth with the superior man’s pursuit of reputation, urging heavenly law, unself-conscious goodness, and TAO.
Discontent asks Complacency, seeks wealth and reputation, and argues that wealth enables good and power while pleasure makes life worthwhile beyond health alone.

A scholar separated from humanity and the world, Complacency defines happiness as contentment, urging the wise to seek sufficiency and reject excess because wealth brings confusion, misery, disease, shame, unhappiness, and fear.

Wealth is pursued for power, influence, and pleasures and requires confidence according to Man Kou Tê. When excessive, it becomes a curse: pursuit and accumulation bring confusion, misery, disease, shame, unhappiness, and fear from thieves and bandits.

leads_to reputation Confidence is described as necessary for securing a place and, through that place, wealth. Man Kou Tê argues that inspiring confidence makes a person conspicuous and can help produce reputation and wealth.
produces happiness Contentment is identified by Complacency as the source of happiness. Too much, especially in wealth, is described as a curse rather than a benefit.

l: Wên Wang of Chao, Chuang Tzŭ
s: Wên Wang of Chao, a prince wielding sovereign power, loves sword-play, fills his halls with swordsmen, watches deadly bouts day and night, and remains dissatisfied.

Swordsmen gather in Wên Wang of Chao’s halls for constant bouts, leaving about a hundred killed or wounded yearly; after the prince accepts Chuang Tzŭ’s teaching, they submit to a new order and die at home.

Heir Apparent Li, a troubled heir apparent with household officers, worries about Chao’s condition, offers silver to secure dismissal of swordsmen, sends for Chuang Tzŭ, and accompanies him before the prince.

is_a sport Sword-play is the activity loved by Wên Wang of Chao, who has swordsmen perform bouts before him day and night. Chuang Tzŭ uses the prince’s interest in sword-play to gain an audience and redirect his attention toward higher forms of sovereign power.

l: sword of the Son of Heaven, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The sword of the Son of Heaven symbolizes the empire: its lands, elements, seasons, and peoples. Made of the five elements and enclosed by the four hordes of barbarians, it operates under Yin and Yang, arbitrating punishment and reward until princes submit.

l: sword of the Princes, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The sword of the Princes symbolically joins the wise, brave, incorruptible, virtuous, loyal, and heroic to model heaven and earth, diffuse peace, and secure obedience.

l: sword of the People, Chuang Tzŭ
s: The sword of the People is a dishevelled, fierce swordsman, like a game-cock, cutting and smiting in personal conflict; Chuang Tzŭ judges it unworthy of a great prince’s sovereign power.

To enable the reader to understand more fully the writings of Chuang Tzŭ, and to appreciate his aim and object, it will be necessary to go back a few more hundred years. In the seventh century B.C., lived a man, now commonly spoken of as Lao Tzŭ. He was the great Prophet of his age. He taught men to return good for evil, and to look forward to a higher life. He professed to have found the clue to all things human and divine. He seems to have insisted that his system could not be reduced to words. Such doctrines as these were, however, not likely to appeal with force to the sympathies of a practical people. In the sixth century B.C., before Lao Tzŭ's death, another Prophet arose. He taught his countrymen that _duty to one's neighbour_ comprises the whole duty of man. Charitableness of heart, justice, sincerity, and fortitude,--sum up the ethics of Confucius. He knew nothing of a God, of a soul, of an unseen world. And he declared that the unknowable had better remain untouched. Against these hard and worldly utterances, Chuang Tzŭ raised a powerful cry. these hard and worldly utterances, Chuang Tzŭ raised a powerful cry. The idealism of Lao Tzŭ had seized upon his poetic soul, and he determined to stem the tide of materialism in which men were being fast rolled to perdition. He failed, of course. It was, indeed, too great a task to persuade the calculating Chinese nation that by doing nothing, all things would be done. But Chuang Tzŭ bequeathed to posterity a work which, by reason of its marvellous literary beauty, has always held a foremost place. It is also a work of much originality of thought. The writer, it is true, appears chiefly as a disciple insisting upon the principles of a Master. But he has contrived to extend the field, and carry his own speculations into regions never dreamt of by Lao Tzŭ. * * * * * It may here be mentioned that the historian Ssŭ-ma Ch'ien, already quoted, states in his notice of Lao Tzŭ that the latter left behind him a small volume in 5,000 and odd characters. But where opinions differ, I have not hesitated to accept that interpretation which seemed to me to be most in harmony with the general tenor of Chuang Tzŭ's philosophy. And where all commentators fail equally, as they sometimes do, to yield anything at all intelligible, I have then ventured to fall back upon what Chuang Tzŭ himself would have called the "light of nature." Always keeping steadily in view the grand precept of Lin Hsi-chung, that we should attempt to interpret Chuang Tzŭ neither according to Lao Tzŭ, nor according to Confucius, nor according to Buddha, but according to Chuang Tzŭ himself. * * * * * Of the thirty-three existing chapters, the first seven are called "inside" chapters, the next fifteen "outside," and the remaining eleven "miscellaneous." "miscellaneous." The meaning of "inside" and "outside" is a matter of dispute. Some Chinese critics have understood these terms in the obvious sense of esoteric and exoteric. But it is simpler to believe with others that the titles of the first seven chapters are taken from the inside or subject-matter, while the outside chapters are so named because their titles are derived casually from words which happen to stand at the beginning or outside of each. Compared with the "miscellaneous," these latter seem to have been classed together as elucidating a single principle in terms more easy of apprehension; while the "miscellaneous" chapters embrace several distinct trains of thought, and are altogether more abstruse. The arrangement is unscientific, and it was probably this which caused Su Tung-p'o to decide that division into chapters belongs to a later age. It has indeed been held that the inside chapters alone (i-vii) are from Chuang Tzŭ's own pen. But most of the other chapters, exclusive of xxix-xxxii, contain unmistakable traces of a master hand. Ch. xvii, by virtue of an exquisite imagery, has earned for its author the affectionate sobriquet of "Chou of the Autumn Floods." * * * * * Chuang Tzŭ, it must be remembered, has been for centuries classed as a heterodox writer. His work was an effort of reaction against the materialism of Confucian teachings. And in the course of it he was anything but sparing of terms. Confucius is dealt with in language which no modern literate can approve. But the beauty and vigour of the language are facts admitted by all. He is constantly quoted in the great standard lexicon which passes under the name of K'ang Hsi. But no acquaintance with the philosophy of Chuang Tzŭ would assist the candidate for honours at the competitive examinations which are the portals to official place and power. Consequently, Chuang Tzŭ is studied chiefly by older men, who have retired from office, or who have been disappointed in their career. Those too who are dominated by a religious craving for something better than mortality, find in his pages much agreeable solace against the troubles of this world, with an implied promise of another and a better world to come. * * * * * It has been publicly announced that translations of Lao Tzŭ and Chuang Tzŭ are to appear among the _Sacred Books of the East_.[17] [17] _The China Review_, vol. xvi, p. 195. Now to include the _Tao-Tê-Ching_ in such a series would be already a doubtful step. Apart from spuriousness, it can only by a severe stretch of courtesy be termed a "sacred book." It undoubtedly contains many of Lao Tzŭ's sayings, but it also undoubtedly contains much that Lao Tzŭ never said and never could have said. It illustrates rather that period when

zŭ's sayings, but it also undoubtedly contains much that Lao Tzŭ never said and never could have said. It illustrates rather that period when the pure TAO of Lao Tzŭ began to be corrupted by alchemistic research and gropings after the elixir of life. It was probably written up in self-defence against the encroachments of Buddhism, in those early days of religious struggle when China was first flooded with the "sacred books" of the West. It is not seriously recognised as the Canon of ancient Taoism. Among the Taoists of to-day, not one in ten thousand has more than heard its name. For modern Taoism is but a hybrid superstition,--a mixture of ancient nature-worship and Buddhistic ceremonial, with TAO as the style of the firm. Its teachings are farther removed from the TAO of Lao Tzŭ than Ritualism from the Christianity of Christ. As to Chuang Tzŭ, his work can in no sense be called "sacred." Unless indeed we modify somewhat the accepted value of terms, and reckon the works of Aristotle among the "sacred" books of the Greeks

." Unless indeed we modify somewhat the accepted value of terms, and reckon the works of Aristotle among the "sacred" books of the Greeks. Chuang Tzŭ was scarcely the founder of a school. He was not a Prophet, as Lao Tzŭ was, nor can he fairly be said ever to have been regarded by genuine Taoists as such. When, many centuries later, the light of Lao Tzŭ's real teachings had long since been obscured, then a foolish Emperor conferred upon Chuang Tzŭ's work the title of _Holy Canon of Nan-hua_.[18] But this was done solely to secure for the follies of the age the sanction of a great name. Not to mention that Lieh Tzŭ's alleged work, and many other similar forgeries have also been equally honoured. So that if works like these are to be included among the _Sacred Books of the East_, then China alone will be able to supply matter for translation for the next few centuries to come.
